name: Canadian French (Laurentian)

allophone_rules.notes: Affrication of /t/ before a high front vocoid (Dow 2019: 1-2; Hall 2016: 2, ex. (2)): petit [pət͡si], têtu [tɛt͡sy].
Affrication of /d/ before a high front vocoid (Dow 2019: 1-2; Hall 2016: 2, ex. (2)): dit [d͡zi], du [d͡zy].
Closed-syllable laxing of /i/ in the final syllable: the coda holds a consonant other than the voiced fricatives /v z ʒ ʁ/ (Hall 2016: 7, ex. (12); Burness et al. 2022: 1-2).
Closed-syllable laxing of /y/ in the final syllable: the coda holds a consonant other than the voiced fricatives /v z ʒ ʁ/ (Hall 2016: 7, ex. (12); Burness et al. 2022: 1-2).
Closed-syllable laxing of /u/ in the final syllable: the coda holds a consonant other than the voiced fricatives /v z ʒ ʁ/ (Hall 2016: 7, ex. (12); Burness et al. 2022: 1-2).

notes: Laurentian French (Quebec and Ontario), as a thin variant of Metropolitan French (fr-FR). It inherits every table, rule and word exception of fr-FR and states only what a cited source states. AFFRICATION: /t d/ before the high front vocoids /i y j ɥ/ are the affricates [t͡s d͡z] (Dow 2019: 1-2, obligatory within words; Hall 2016: 2, ex. (2), after Burstynsky 1968: 13: petit [pət͡si], têtu [tɛt͡sy], dit [d͡zi]). The trigger list holds the glide-initial units the grapheme table has: ⟨ien⟩ [jɛ̃] and the glides [j ɥ]. LAXING: in the final syllable, /i y u/ are lax [ɪ ʏ ʊ] before a closing consonant other than the voiced fricatives /v z ʒ ʁ/ (Hall 2016: 7, ex. (11)-(12), after Walker 1984: 56 and Poliquin 2006; Burness et al. 2022: 1-2: élite [elɪt], annule [anʏl], égoutte [egʊt]); the final syllable is the last nucleus (followed_by_nucleus false) and the closing consonant is the next surface phoneme, so a silent final letter (petit, petits) does not close it. /a/ ~ /ɑ/: Laurentian French keeps the contrast (Burness et al. 2022: 1: patte [pat], pâte [pɑt]); fr-FR already maps ⟨â⟩ to /ɑ/, so nothing changes. NOT MODELLED (no cited source states the contexts the engine can see, or the engine cannot see them): laxing before a consonant cluster that starts with /v z ʒ ʁ/ and laxing before a final consonant cluster in general (a silent final letter, as in sourd, looks like a consonant to the rule layer), lengthening of the tense high vowels before final /v z ʒ ʁ/ (Hall 2016: 7, ex. (13)) because a silent final ⟨e⟩ hides the word edge (église), laxing harmony and optional laxing in non-final syllables (Hall 2016: 7-8), laxing of /i y u/ spelled with a digraph, the nasal vowel values, vowel length and lengthening before /v z ʒ ʁ/ for the other vowels, final-consonant clusters, the colloquial [mwɛ] [twɛ] for moi and toi, and affrication in a whole-word exception inherited from fr-FR, which bypasses the rules: cactus, jadis, gratis and métis keep [t d] before [i y], where the rule within words gives [t͡s d͡z] (Dow 2019: 1-2). Acadian French is a different variety and affrication is largely absent from it (Dow 2019: 2).

sources.author: Hall, D.C.
sources.title: Contrast and phonological activity in the vowel system of Laurentian French
sources.notes: READ (open access PDF). Ex. (2), p. 2, after Burstynsky (1968: 13): assibilation of /t/ and /d/ before /i/ and /y/ (petit [p(ə)tsi], têtu [tɛtsy], j'ai dit [ʒedzi], du pain [dzypɛ̃]). §3.1, p. 7, after Walker (1984: 56) and Poliquin (2006: 6, 102): in the final syllable the high vowels /i y u/ are lax [ɪ ʏ ʊ] when the coda has a consonant other than the voiced fricatives /v z ʒ ʁ/ (élite [elɪt], annule [anʏl], égoutte [egʊt]) and tense in an open final syllable (béni [beni], début [deby], dégoût [degu]).

sources.author: Dow, M.
sources.title: Subsegmental interactions between affrication and devoicing in Québec French
sources.publisher: Actes du congrès annuel de l'Association canadienne de linguistique 2019
sources.notes: READ (open access PDF). p. 1: affrication is the fricative-like release of the coronal stops /t, d/ before the high front vocoids /i, j, y, ɥ/ (after Dumas 1987), written [ts, dz]. p. 2: it is obligatory within words, varies little with social class, and occurs in almost all areas of Québec (Charlevoix is more variable).

sources.author: Burness, P., Tahtadjian, T., MacLeod, B. & Ahn, S.
sources.title: Vowel laxing in Laurentian French: lowering, centralization, and individual variation
sources.publisher: Actes du congrès annuel de l'Association canadienne de linguistique 2022
sources.notes: READ (open access PDF). p. 1: Laurentian French (Ontario and Québec) has a phonemic /a/ ~ /ɑ/ contrast (patte [pat], pâte [pɑt]), affrication of /t, d/ before /i, y/, and laxing of /i y u/ before certain coda consonants in closed syllables (Poliquin 2006); the process is obligatory in final syllables.

ancestors.notes: Standard Metropolitan French, the base of every other variety here.
